evaluation.positioning_hook: After her ex-boyfriend is murdered at school, a grieving teen digs into a buried campus death and discovers the killer may be an inhuman predator hiding in plain sight.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The core promise is immediate: a teen murder mystery that turns into a predator hunt, with grief as the emotional engine. The audience is clear and genre-native, though the school setting and serialized-feeling mythology narrow it more than a broad four-quadrant feature.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: Ryan’s murder, the old Lillian Crawford case, and Macy’s decision to investigate are all legible quickly. The hook gets stronger once Lillian appears as a literal threat, but the script is still early in defining the exact rules of the mystery.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Macy has a usable emotional engine — guilt, anger, and determination — and the Outlanders give her a social orbit. The supporting cast is vivid in attitude, but most of them are still defined by function rather than distinct inner contradiction.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The teen-clique-plus-murder setup is familiar, but the wealthy-school texture and the turn toward a supernatural predator give it a cleaner ownable edge. The execution is still leaning on recognizable genre beats rather than a fully singular voice.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening murder, assembly reveal, and warehouse kill create clear escalation, and the ending pushes the mystery forward. The middle spends a lot of time on grief and social atmosphere before the investigation really takes over.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script has a fresh enough collision of teen social hierarchy, murder mystery, and monster threat to feel marketable. What keeps it from a higher band is that the underlying shape still reads like a familiar horror-investigation engine.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The affluent suburban school, the Outlanders clique, and the old campus legend give the world some social specificity. It is still mostly a container for the mystery rather than a fully rule-bound ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script is aiming for glossy teen melodrama colliding with horror violence, and that contrast is readable on the page. The tonal identity is consistent, but it has not yet landed on a truly hard-to-imitate signature.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Lillian Crawford and the closed police report suggest a deeper mythology beneath the immediate murder plot. The page hints at more than it reveals, but the deeper layer is still mostly promise rather than payoff.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Outlanders have a built-in social engine, and Macy’s grief gives the group a reason to fracture under pressure. Still, the relationships are currently more archetypal than combustible, so the ensemble energy is present but not yet rich.

lead_characters.name: Macy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16-17, high-school student, affluent suburban background
lead_characters.hook: Macy is the emotional center of the script: outwardly polished, socially fluent, and quick with a joke, but internally cracked open by guilt after Ryan’s murder. She starts as the girl trying to keep her morning normal and becomes the one person willing to chase the truth, even when grief curdles into obsession. Her contradiction is the engine — she wants to stay bright and social, but the story keeps pulling her toward rage, isolation, and a darker kind of resolve.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a lead in a teen prestige horror role like Willa Fitzgerald in Scream or Sophie Nélisse in Yellowjackets — a performance that gets to pivot from charm to raw grief to feral determination. It gives an actor a full emotional runway, plus the chance to carry both the social-clique scenes and the investigative horror turn.

lead_characters.name: Jessica
lead_characters.hook: Jessica is the polished, socially strategic friend who reads as supportive but also tracks the room and the hierarchy at all times. She has enough warmth to keep Macy close and enough self-awareness to feel like she knows more than she says, which makes her useful both as confidante and pressure point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the sharp, scene-stealing social intelligence of a supporting player in Mean Girls or Yellowjackets — the friend who can turn from comic sparkle to quiet alarm in a beat. It offers fashion, status, and emotional subtext without needing to carry the whole film.

lead_characters.name: Kyle
lead_characters.hook: Kyle is the confident, smirking alpha of the group, the one who performs ease even when the room turns tense. He reads as the guy who can joke through danger, but the murder and the Lillian talk start to expose a more brittle, reactive layer underneath.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is good territory for the charismatic teen male supporting turn that actors get in Scream or Riverdale-adjacent ensemble horror — the role that lets someone play swagger, fear, and suspicion in the same package. It’s a useful showcase for timing and social dominance.

lead_characters.name: Nina
lead_characters.hook: Nina is the sarcastic observer, the one who weaponizes wit to stay a step removed from the emotional mess. She has the cleanest line into the group’s skepticism and fear, which makes her feel like a pressure-release valve and a possible truth-teller.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of dry, cutting supporting role that gives an actor the best lines and the chance to steal scenes the way a sharp ensemble player does in Buffy or Yellowjackets. It’s a compact showcase for comic timing with a darker undercurrent.

lead_characters.name: Ethan
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the easygoing jokester whose humor starts to fail as the deaths stack up. He functions as the group’s social lubricant, but the script also gives him enough fear and guilt to suggest he may not stay light for long.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play the pivot from comic relief to shaken witness, similar to the best ensemble teen-horror supporting turns. It gives him room to be likable first, then destabilized.

lead_characters.name: Gabby
lead_characters.hook: Gabby is Macy’s younger brother and the script’s innocence valve, but he also becomes a useful witness when he mentions the hooded figure outside the house. He brings domestic normalcy into the horror plot and quietly widens the threat beyond school.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean child-supporting role with a memorable beat and a strong fear-response scene. It gives a young actor a clear, emotionally legible function in the story.

lead_characters.name: Lillian Crawford
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late teens/young adult, supernatural threat
lead_characters.hook: Lillian is the buried campus legend who becomes the story’s literal predator: dead, rumored, and then violently real in the warehouse attack. She carries the mythology of the old case and the physical menace of the present-day killer, making her the script’s most distinctive horror element.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of villain role that can become a calling card — the silent, inhuman, physically expressive antagonist that recalls the best creature-adjacent horror turns. It gives an actor or performer a chance to create iconography, not just dialogue.

lead_characters.name: Principal Hawthorne
lead_characters.hook: Principal Hawthorne is the institutional face of the story’s public crisis, the man forced to announce Ryan’s murder and manage the school’s panic. He’s not a mystery engine so much as the authority figure who makes the horror official.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong character-actor role in the tradition of the worried administrator in teen thrillers and horror. It gives an actor a single high-stakes public scene with emotional authority.

lead_characters.name: Mom
lead_characters.hook: Macy’s mother is the warm domestic counterweight to the violence outside the house. She’s written as supportive and observant, which gives the home scenes emotional grounding even when Macy is spiraling.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded parent role that lets an actor play concern, restraint, and helplessness with real emotional weight. It’s a reliable supporting showcase in a genre piece.

lead_characters.name: Dad
lead_characters.hook: Macy’s father is the calm, ordinary presence in the kitchen scenes, a stabilizing figure who underscores how violently the story invades normal life. He’s functional but useful as part of the family baseline.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a concise, naturalistic parent role that gives an actor a few grounded beats without needing heavy exposition. It’s the kind of part that adds texture to a genre ensemble.

casting_characteristics: one teen female lead carrying grief and investigation
one supernatural antagonist with physical menace

technical.vfx_details: A few crash and blood-enhancement moments, plus possible subtle supernatural enhancement for Lillian’s speed/appearance; no large-scale effects footprint is implied on the page.
technical.sfx_needs: practical blood, body injury makeup, tire blowout/car crash beats, severed-head reveal in a box, and a creature-style attack sequence

rights_flags.detail: "Happier Than Ever" by Billie Eilish is used in the opening limo sequence.
"When the Party’s Over" by Billie Eilish is used in the auditorium announcement and again in Macy’s bedroom.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: teen horror mystery with a theatrical-to-streaming path and strong genre-platform fit.

budget.note: Contemporary school and home locations keep the footprint contained, but the limo crash, warehouse kill, severed-head box reveal, and repeated night exteriors add practical effects and stunt coordination that can push above a very lean indie plan.

casting.note: The lead needs to carry grief, suspicion, and investigative momentum while still reading as socially effortless; Lillian also needs a performer with strong physical menace. The teen ensemble is accessible, but those two roles are the real lift.

development.note: The script has a clear horror-mystery spine, but the mythology around Lillian Crawford is still more teased than defined, so buyers will want the rules of the threat and the Ryan/Lillian connection sharpened before a greenlight conversation.

comp_set.title: Scream
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen social dynamics, murder fallout, and a killer who turns a high-school ecosystem into a suspicion machine.

comp_set.title: I Know What You Did Last Summer
comp_set.why_it_comps: Grief-driven teen mystery with a body-count engine and a past crime that keeps resurfacing.

comp_set.title: Yellowjackets
comp_set.why_it_comps: The blend of teen clique pressure, buried trauma, and a dark mythology underneath the social surface.

comp_set.title: Totally Killer
comp_set.why_it_comps: High-school horror energy with a playful social texture and a murder mystery built around a past death.

audience_target.primary_audience: Teen and young-adult horror audiences who want school-set mystery, grief, and a female-led predator story.
audience_target.demographics: Skews F18-34, with secondary pull for M18-34 and older genre fans who follow teen horror franchises.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, a small teen ensemble, and limited practical effects keep it in indie feature territory, though the car crash and creature attack sequences require disciplined scope control.

types_of_buyers: indie financiers looking for elevated teen IP
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where school-set horror, female-led suspense, and social-clique dynamics are the selling points. The script has enough hook for a streamer and enough contained scope for a producer looking to launch a filmmaker.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature as written; the Lillian mythology suggests more world, but there is not yet a clear spinoff vector with a separate anchor character or universe lane.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Macy has a clean emotional engine.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a lead role buyers can package around: grief, guilt, and determination all live in the same part. Actors and managers will respond to a role that can play vulnerable, socially sharp, and increasingly dangerous in one arc.
strengths.evidence: Her reaction to Ryan’s death, the guilt over not calling him back, and the late-night research montage all push her from heartbreak into obsession.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The school setting turns into a suspicion machine.
strengths.what_it_means: That creates a built-in commercial engine because every hallway, classroom, and clique interaction can carry threat. Buyers looking for contained genre with social texture will see a clear lane for tension without needing a huge world build.
strengths.evidence: The assembly announcement, the Outlanders’ public grief, and the whispered fear after Ryan’s murder all weaponize the campus environment.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Lillian is a strong horror-image antagonist.
strengths.what_it_means: A physically expressive, inhuman killer gives the film iconography and a marketable threat beyond the mystery itself. That’s the kind of villain concept that can sell posters, trailers, and word-of-mouth.
strengths.evidence: The warehouse attack turns Lillian from rumor into a silent, fast, brutal predator.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The opening murder is immediate and cinematic.
strengths.what_it_means: The script announces its genre promise fast, which helps a buyer understand the movie in one pass and helps a trailer cut itself. It also signals a production that knows how to stage a set-piece early.
strengths.evidence: Ryan’s limo ambush, tire blowout, and violent crash establish danger before the story settles into school life.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The teen ensemble has usable social chemistry.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the film more than a solo lead; it creates a group dynamic that can generate banter, suspicion, and fracture. Ensemble chemistry is a real asset for casting conversations and for audience rewatch value.
strengths.evidence: The Outlanders’ morning walk, teasing, and then collective shock at the assembly give the group a recognizable rhythm.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, female-led teen horror mystery with a clear emotional spine and a villain image that can do real marketing work. The school setting, small ensemble, and contemporary footprint keep it in an accessible indie lane, while Macy’s grief-to-obsession arc gives buyers a role worth packaging around.

items.area: The mythology is still more tease than engine.
items.detail: Lillian Crawford, the old police report, and the campus rumor all point to a deeper backstory, but the rules of the threat are still vague on the page. That makes the project feel promising rather than fully buy-ready, because the buyer is being asked to trust the mystery before the mystery has a shape.

items.area: The opening reads like a pilot, not a feature.
items.detail: The script is labeled as a feature, but the page count and structure currently play like the first act of a serialized teen horror story: school introduction, clique setup, inciting death, then a new body at the end. A buyer will notice that the feature engine is still in setup mode.

items.area: The supporting teens are archetypes first.
items.detail: Jessica, Kyle, Nina, and Ethan each have a clear social function, but their inner lives are still thin relative to Macy’s. That keeps the ensemble from feeling fully combustible and limits the upside of the group scenes beyond banter and reaction.

items.area: The Billie Eilish needle-drops need clearance.
items.detail: "Happier Than Ever" and "When the Party’s Over" are both named and structurally important to the opening and the assembly sequence. That creates a real sync-clearance and budget conversation before any buyer can treat the scenes as locked.

issues.headline: The biggest friction is that the script is selling a larger mythology than it has yet fully defined, so the buyer is being asked to lean on promise. The feature also still plays with a pilot-like setup rhythm, and the named Billie Eilish tracks add a real clearance line item on top of that development uncertainty.
